title: What are brands and why do they matter?
speaker: Justin Papps

beats.say: Week three. Why do brands matter? Justin Papps from Tenet defines a brand as beliefs and perceptions that create a positive predisposition at the point of choice.

board.title: What are **brands** and why do they matter?
board.name: Justin Papps

beats.say: So a brand lives in the customer's head, not your guidelines, and the work happens before purchase. Marketing is persuasion.
Brand first meant to burn. Then the mark showed ownership, then who made it, then a reputation for quality. Now it means what it says about you.
Associations cluster around the founder, what the company does, and adjectives. Tesla shows the founder link cuts both ways. Keep the link positive and consistent.
Brand exposures went from ten to twenty a day in the seventeen hundreds to ten thousand today, and our brains haven't grown. The battle moved from the aisle to a phone screen.
Five reasons brands matter: economic engines, behavioural shortcuts, strategy in action, shaping culture, and volatility moats.
One, economic engines. A Louis Vuitton backpack costs fifteen point six times a Maverick and Co bag that beats it on compartments and warranty.
An iPhone costs about four hundred and fifty to make and sells for up to sixteen hundred, a margin of sixty-seven percent plus. If brands didn't matter, Amazon would list products alphabetically.
Two, behavioural shortcuts. Kahneman's System One is about ninety-five percent of thinking: fast and unconscious. System Two is slow and logical, for big decisions. Brands aim at System One.
Brand strategy rests on four pillars: relevance, distinctiveness, consistency and availability. Land all four and you get cut-through and salience.
Distinctive assets compound with age. But Ipsos found a paradox: logos are in ninety-four percent of ads and return one point four times. Sonic cues are in six percent and return eight point five.
Three, strategy in action. Segmentation, targeting and positioning are business decisions with trade-offs. Get them right for a positive return on marketing investment.
Four, brands shape culture. Harley-Davidson, Nike's Kaepernick ad and the RTA speeding campaign work. Pepsi's Kendall Jenner ad failed, borrowing a movement it had no standing in.
Five, volatility moats: equity, reputation and crisis response. Tesla broke all three. Volkswagen survived Dieselgate on equity alone. KFC's FCK bucket rebuilt equity.
Consumer equity grows most through referral from family and friends. Stop advertising and you fade from memory, and getting back costs more than holding on.
An unknown laptop brand can have the best specs and still no trust. Brands must be machine readable and human loveable, not AI slop.
Marketing is a long game, often two to three years. Sampling breaks the uncertainty barrier. And in B2B, lean on the rational case and keep clear promises.
So win before the point of choice, and audit your assets. Attention is cheap. Memory is expensive. Preference is priceless. That's week three.
